Diagnostics and likelihood

A filter that runs is not a filter that works. The functions in this chapter ask whether an assimilation is statistically healthy. They detect a wrong covariance, a wrong amount of inflation or too small an ensemble, and they do not fix any of them. All of them are pure functions of arrays you already have, so they cost little and own no state.

One statement organises the chapter. If the forecast and the noise are correctly specified, the innovation is a draw from N(0,Σy)\mathcal{N}(\vect{0}, \gmat{\Sigma}_y)N(0,Σy​) and the truth is one more member of the ensemble. Each diagnostic is a different projection of that statement. For each one this chapter gives the value it should take, the finite-ensemble correction to that value, and how it fails. Those corrections matter: in the toy problem below, a calibrated ensemble of 10 members with 3 observations has a χ2/Dy\chi^2 / D_yχ2/Dy​ of about 1.3.

The innovation and its covariance¶

Everything starts from the part of the observation that the forecast did not predict. With the forecast members mapped to h(e)=h(x(e))\vect{h}^{(e)} = h(\vect{x}^{(e)})h(e)=h(x(e)), the innovation rˉ∈RDy\bar{\vect{r}} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y}rˉ∈RDy​ and the covariance Σ^y∈RDy×Dy\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times D_y}Σ^y​∈RDy​×Dy​ are

rˉ=y−hˉ,Σ^y=Σ^h+Σε.\bar{\vect{r}} = \vect{y} - \bar{\vect{h}}, \qquad \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y = \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_h + \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon.rˉ=y−hˉ,Σ^y​=Σ^h​+Σε​.
(13.1)

filterax.utils.innovation computes the first, and innovation_covariance the second as a gaussx.LowRankUpdate. Two normalisations follow. normalized_innovation divides each component by its own standard deviation, so it uses only the diagonal. innovation_statistics whitens with the principal inverse root, which uses all of Σ^y\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yΣ^y​:

rˉi[Σ^y]ii,rˉwh=Σ^y−1/2rˉ.\frac{\bar{r}_i}{\sqrt{[\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y]_{ii}}}, \qquad \bar{\vect{r}}_\text{wh} = \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y^{-1/2} \bar{\vect{r}}.[Σ^y​]ii​​rˉi​​,rˉwh​=Σ^y−1/2​rˉ.
(13.2)

The first has components near N(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0, 1)N(0,1) that can still be correlated, and the second should be close to N(0,I)\mathcal{N}(\vect{0}, \mat{I})N(0,I). A Cholesky factor would also whiten, but its result depends on the order of the observations. The principal root does not, so a permuted observation vector gives the same whitened residual, permuted.

The likelihood¶

The innovation likelihood is both a diagnostic and the training signal of chapter 14:

log⁡N(rˉ;0,Σ^y)=−12(Dylog⁡2π+log⁡∣Σ^y∣+rˉ⊤Σ^y−1rˉ).\log \mathcal{N}(\bar{\vect{r}}; \vect{0}, \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y) = -\frac{1}{2} \left(D_y \log 2 \pi + \log \vert \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y \vert + \bar{\vect{r}}^\top \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y^{-1} \bar{\vect{r}}\right).logN(rˉ;0,Σ^y​)=−21​(Dy​log2π+log∣Σ^y​∣+rˉ⊤Σ^y−1​rˉ).
(13.3)

log_likelihood evaluates it for any operator through gaussx dispatch. On a LowRankUpdate that means the matrix-determinant lemma and Woodbury, at O(NE2Dy+NE3)O(N_\mathcal{E}^2 D_y + N_\mathcal{E}^3)O(NE2​Dy​+NE3​). With NE>DyN_\mathcal{E} > D_yNE​>Dy​ the filters and innovation_statistics take a thin QR of the stacked factors [U,Σε1/2][\mat{U}, \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{1/2}][U,Σε1/2​] instead, where U=H~⊤/NE−1\mat{U} = \tilde{\mat{H}}^\top / \sqrt{N_\mathcal{E} - 1}U=H~⊤/NE​−1​, at O(NEDy2)O(N_\mathcal{E} D_y^2)O(NE​Dy2​). That route gives the triangular T\mat{T}T with T⊤T=Σ^y\mat{T}^\top \mat{T} = \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yT⊤T=Σ^y​ without squaring a condition number. The log-determinant then comes off the diagonal of T\mat{T}T.

Program 13.1 computes all of this on one forecast and checks it against a dense reference.

The first line prints 0e+00, so utils.innovation and the innovation key agree. The next two print [-0.878 -0.897 0.52 ] for the per-component form and [-0.807 -0.954 0.704] for the whitened one. They differ because Σ^y\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yΣ^y​ has off-diagonal entries. The line 2.05616259 2.05616259 0.68539 holds χ2\chi^2χ2 from a solve, the squared norm of the whitened residual and χ2/Dy\chi^2 / D_yχ2/Dy​. All three log-likelihoods and the numpy reference print -4.50287410, and so does analysis.log_likelihood. Reordering the observations changes the principal-root residual only by a permutation, to 1e-16, while the Cholesky residual changes by up to 0.33.

Chi-squared consistency¶

Contracting rˉ\bar{\vect{r}}rˉ against Σ^y−1\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y^{-1}Σ^y−1​ gives the classic consistency statistic Mehra, 1970:

χ2=rˉ⊤Σ^y−1rˉ,E[χ2]=Dy,V[χ2]=2Dy.\chi^2 = \bar{\vect{r}}^\top \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y^{-1} \bar{\vect{r}}, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\chi^2] = D_y, \qquad \mathbb{V}[\chi^2] = 2 D_y.χ2=rˉ⊤Σ^y−1​rˉ,E[χ2]=Dy​,V[χ2]=2Dy​.
(13.4)

Its two forms are chi2_consistency and chi2_normalized, which returns χ2/Dy\chi^2 / D_yχ2/Dy​ with a target of 1 and a null standard deviation of 2/Dy\sqrt{2 / D_y}2/Dy​​. Both take Σ^y−1rˉ\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y^{-1} \bar{\vect{r}}Σ^y−1​rˉ already solved, so they use whichever solver produced the analysis. A value that stays above 1 means an overconfident, underdispersive filter, which needs inflation (chapter 12), and a value below 1 means an overdispersive one.

The finite-ensemble correction¶

(13.4) holds when Σ^y\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yΣ^y​ is the true covariance of rˉ\bar{\vect{r}}rˉ, and an ensemble breaks that in two ways. The mean hˉ\bar{\vect{h}}hˉ has its own sampling error, which adds Σh/NE\gmat{\Sigma}_h / N_\mathcal{E}Σh​/NE​ to the covariance of rˉ\bar{\vect{r}}rˉ. And the inverse is a convex function, so the inverse of a noisy Σ^y\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yΣ^y​ is too large on average. Both push χ2/Dy\chi^2 / D_yχ2/Dy​ above 1 for a perfectly calibrated filter.

It prints 1.273, 1.054 and 1.005 for NE=10N_\mathcal{E} = 10NE​=10, 40 and 200, and 0.816 for the null standard deviation 2/3\sqrt{2 / 3}2/3​ of one window. So a calibrated 10-member ensemble reads about 1.27 here. Tuning inflation until the statistic reaches exactly 1 would ask for more spread than a calibrated filter has. The correction fades as NEN_\mathcal{E}NE​ grows, and NE≫DyN_\mathcal{E} \gg D_yNE​≫Dy​ is the case where (13.4) can be read directly.

Spread and skill¶

The per-variable spread σi=[Σ^x]ii\sigma_i = \sqrt{[\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x]_{ii}}σi​=[Σ^x​]ii​​ is ensemble_spread, and rms_spread reduces it to one number. A collapsing spread warns of filter divergence, and it needs no truth at all.

In a twin experiment the truth xtrue\vect{x}_\text{true}xtrue​ is known, so rmse_vs_truth gives the error of the mean, and spread_skill_ratio compares the two Whitaker & Loughe, 1998:

RMSE=1Dx∑i(xˉi−xtrue,i)2,SSR=1Dx∑iσi2RMSE.\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{D_x} \sum_i (\bar{x}_i - x_{\text{true}, i})^2}, \qquad \mathrm{SSR} = \frac{\sqrt{\frac{1}{D_x} \sum_i \sigma_i^2}}{\mathrm{RMSE}}.RMSE=Dx​1​i∑​(xˉi​−xtrue,i​)2​,SSR=RMSEDx​1​∑i​σi2​​​.
(13.5)

SSR<1\mathrm{SSR} < 1SSR<1 means underdispersive, and SSR>1\mathrm{SSR} > 1SSR>1 overdispersive.

The target is not exactly 1 Fortin et al., 2014. If the truth and the members are exchangeable with variance σ2\sigma^2σ2, the mean xˉ\bar{x}xˉ has variance σ2/NE\sigma^2 / N_\mathcal{E}σ2/NE​ and is independent of the truth. So E[(xˉ−xtrue)2]=σ2(1+1/NE)\mathbb{E}[(\bar{x} - x_\text{true})^2] = \sigma^2 (1 + 1 / N_\mathcal{E})E[(xˉ−xtrue​)2]=σ2(1+1/NE​), and the calibrated value is

SSRcalibrated=NENE+1.\mathrm{SSR}_\text{calibrated} = \sqrt{\frac{N_\mathcal{E}}{N_\mathcal{E} + 1}}.SSRcalibrated​=NE​+1NE​​​.
(13.6)

The ratio also needs care across time. spread_skill_ratio works on one window, and the mean of those ratios is biased upwards, so pool the squares of the spread and the error first.

It prints:

Rank histograms¶

A rank histogram tests the whole distribution and not just its second moment Hamill, 2001. For each variable and each window, rank_histogram counts how many of the NEN_\mathcal{E}NE​ members lie strictly below the truth, which gives a rank in {0,…,NE}\{0, \dots, N_\mathcal{E}\}{0,…,NE​}. If the truth is exchangeable with the members, every one of the NE+1N_\mathcal{E} + 1NE​+1 ranks is equally likely. A U shape means the truth often falls outside the ensemble, so it is underdispersive. A dome means overdispersive, and a slope means a bias.

rank_histogram_chi2 turns flatness into one number, with OkO_kOk​ the count in bin kkk:

χrank2=∑k(Ok−Ek)2Ek,Ek=NtotalNbins.\chi^2_\text{rank} = \sum_k \frac{(O_k - E_k)^2}{E_k}, \qquad E_k = \frac{N_\text{total}}{N_\text{bins}}.χrank2​=k∑​Ek​(Ok​−Ek​)2​,Ek​=Nbins​Ntotal​​.
(13.7)

Under a uniform null with independent counts this is χ2\chi^2χ2 with Nbins−1N_\text{bins} - 1Nbins​−1 degrees of freedom, so its expectation is Nbins−1=NEN_\text{bins} - 1 = N_\mathcal{E}Nbins​−1=NE​.

With NE=9N_\mathcal{E} = 9NE​=9 there are 10 bins, and the null expectation of χrank2\chi^2_\text{rank}χrank2​ is 9.

CaseCountsχrank2\chi^2_\text{rank}χrank2​
calibrated[420 392 410 415 393 382 390 416 366 416]7.3
underdispersive, members with half the spread[985 325 277 241 213 208 220 239 348 944]2042.6

The shapes are as described above. Two entries warn about use. Verifying against noisy observations gives a false U from a calibrated ensemble until the members carry the same noise. And the counts must be independent. The same calibrated forecast with two copied components prints as copied 32.2, far above the null of 9, with no calibration problem at all. Neighbouring sites and successive windows of a real run are correlated in the same way, if less extremely.

CRPS¶

The continuous ranked probability score is a strictly proper scoring rule for a forecast distribution against one scalar Gneiting & Raftery, 2007. It rewards both calibration and sharpness. It compares the forecast distribution function FFF with a step at the observation yyy:

CRPS=∫(F(x)−1{x≥y})2dx=E∣x−y∣−12E∣x−x′∣,\mathrm{CRPS} = \int \left(F(x) - \mathbb{1}\{x \ge y\}\right)^2 \mathrm{d} x = \mathbb{E} \vert x - y \vert - \frac{1}{2} \mathbb{E} \vert x - x' \vert,CRPS=∫(F(x)−1{x≥y})2dx=E∣x−y∣−21​E∣x−x′∣,
(13.8)

for independent draws xxx and x′x'x′ from FFF, and it has the units of yyy. Lower is better. Hersbach (2000) studies it for ensembles, with FFF the empirical distribution of the members.

The double sum in the second term has a one-line reduction. Take the sorted members x(1)≤⋯≤x(NE)x_{(1)} \le \dots \le x_{(N_\mathcal{E})}x(1)​≤⋯≤x(NE​)​. The value x(e)x_{(e)}x(e)​ appears with a plus sign against the e−1e - 1e−1 smaller members, and with a minus sign against the NE−eN_\mathcal{E} - eNE​−e larger ones, so

12E∣x−x′∣=12NE2∑e,e′∣x(e)−x(e′)∣=1NE2∑e(2e−1−NE) x(e),\frac{1}{2} \mathbb{E} \vert x - x' \vert = \frac{1}{2 N_\mathcal{E}^2} \sum_{e, e'} \vert x^{(e)} - x^{(e')} \vert = \frac{1}{N_\mathcal{E}^2} \sum_e (2 e - 1 - N_\mathcal{E}) \, x_{(e)},21​E∣x−x′∣=2NE2​1​e,e′∑​∣x(e)−x(e′)∣=NE2​1​e∑​(2e−1−NE​)x(e)​,
(13.9)

which crps_ensemble evaluates at O(NElog⁡NE)O(N_\mathcal{E} \log N_\mathcal{E})O(NE​logNE​), and crps_ensemble_batch averages it over an observation vector.

The sum over e,e′e, e'e,e′ includes the pairs e=e′e = e'e=e′, so the ensemble score is larger than that of the distribution it samples. For a calibrated Gaussian forecast with unit variance, E∣x−y∣=2/π\mathbb{E} \vert x - y \vert = 2 / \sqrt{\pi}E∣x−y∣=2/π​ and the second term is (1−1/NE)/π(1 - 1 / N_\mathcal{E}) / \sqrt{\pi}(1−1/NE​)/π​, which gives

E[CRPS]=1π(1+1NE).\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{CRPS}] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \left(1 + \frac{1}{N_\mathcal{E}}\right).E[CRPS]=π​1​(1+NE​1​).
(13.10)

So scores from ensembles of different sizes are not directly comparable.

The first line prints 0.233546 0.233546 0.233531, so the sorted identity matches the double sum exactly and the integral to the resolution of its grid. The means print 0.618 0.621 at NE=10N_\mathcal{E} = 10NE​=10 and 0.575 0.578 at NE=40N_\mathcal{E} = 40NE​=40, close to (13.10). The batch form prints 0.375, the mean of 0.25 and 0.5.

Desroziers diagnostics¶

A long record of departures lets you read the error covariances off in observation space Desroziers et al., 2005. Write rˉt∣t−1=y−Hxˉt∣t−1\bar{\vect{r}}_{t \mid t-1} = \vect{y} - \mat{H} \bar{\vect{x}}_{t \mid t-1}rˉt∣t−1​=y−Hxˉt∣t−1​ for the forecast departure, the innovation, and rˉt∣t=y−Hxˉt∣t\bar{\vect{r}}_{t \mid t} = \vect{y} - \mat{H} \bar{\vect{x}}_{t \mid t}rˉt∣t​=y−Hxˉt∣t​ for the analysis departure. Both are in RDy\mathbb{R}^{D_y}RDy​.

The derivation takes three lines. The analysis mean is xˉt∣t=xˉt∣t−1+Grˉt∣t−1\bar{\vect{x}}_{t \mid t} = \bar{\vect{x}}_{t \mid t-1} + \mat{G} \bar{\vect{r}}_{t \mid t-1}xˉt∣t​=xˉt∣t−1​+Grˉt∣t−1​, and I−HG=ΣεΣy−1\mat{I} - \mat{H} \mat{G} = \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon \gmat{\Sigma}_y^{-1}I−HG=Σε​Σy−1​, so

rˉt∣t=ΣεΣy−1rˉt∣t−1.\bar{\vect{r}}_{t \mid t} = \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon \gmat{\Sigma}_y^{-1} \bar{\vect{r}}_{t \mid t-1}.rˉt∣t​=Σε​Σy−1​rˉt∣t−1​.
(13.11)

If the filter’s Σy\gmat{\Sigma}_yΣy​ is the true covariance of rˉt∣t−1\bar{\vect{r}}_{t \mid t-1}rˉt∣t−1​, multiplying out gives the three statistics filterax accumulates:

E[rˉt∣t−1rˉt∣t−1⊤]=Σy,E[rˉt∣trˉt∣t−1⊤]=Σε,E[rˉt∣trˉt∣t⊤]=ΣεΣy−1Σε=Σε−HΣx∣yH⊤.\mathbb{E}\left[\bar{\vect{r}}_{t \mid t-1} \bar{\vect{r}}_{t \mid t-1}^\top\right] = \gmat{\Sigma}_y, \qquad \mathbb{E}\left[\bar{\vect{r}}_{t \mid t} \bar{\vect{r}}_{t \mid t-1}^\top\right] = \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon, \qquad \mathbb{E}\left[\bar{\vect{r}}_{t \mid t} \bar{\vect{r}}_{t \mid t}^\top\right] = \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon \gmat{\Sigma}_y^{-1} \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon = \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon - \mat{H} \gmat{\Sigma}_{x \mid y} \mat{H}^\top.E[rˉt∣t−1​rˉt∣t−1⊤​]=Σy​,E[rˉt∣t​rˉt∣t−1⊤​]=Σε​,E[rˉt∣t​rˉt∣t⊤​]=Σε​Σy−1​Σε​=Σε​−HΣx∣y​H⊤.
(13.12)

These are desroziers_innovation_cov, desroziers_R_estimate and desroziers_analysis_residual_cov, each an average over the TTT windows of an array with shape (T,Dy)(T, D_y)(T,Dy​). The middle one is the most useful. Subtracting it from the first estimates HΣxH⊤\mat{H} \gmat{\Sigma}_x \mat{H}^\topHΣx​H⊤, so one record separates forecast error from observation error.

If the filter assumed Σεused\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^\text{used}Σεused​ and Σyused\gmat{\Sigma}_y^\text{used}Σyused​, then the same algebra gives

E[rˉt∣trˉt∣t−1⊤]=Σεused(Σyused)−1Σy,\mathbb{E}\left[\bar{\vect{r}}_{t \mid t} \bar{\vect{r}}_{t \mid t-1}^\top\right] = \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^\text{used} \left(\gmat{\Sigma}_y^\text{used}\right)^{-1} \gmat{\Sigma}_y,E[rˉt∣t​rˉt∣t−1⊤​]=Σεused​(Σyused​)−1Σy​,
(13.13)

which is neither the true nor the assumed noise, and in practice it moves the assumed value towards the true one.

Degrees of freedom for signal¶

How much did the observations constrain the analysis? The degrees of freedom for signal is the trace of the influence of the observations on the analysis in observation space Cardinali et al., 2004:

DFS=tr(GH)=tr(Σε−1HΣx∣yH⊤).\mathrm{DFS} = \op{tr}(\mat{G} \mat{H}) = \op{tr}\left(\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} \mat{H} \gmat{\Sigma}_{x \mid y} \mat{H}^\top\right).DFS=tr(GH)=tr(Σε−1​HΣx∣y​H⊤).
(13.14)

The second form uses G=Σx∣yH⊤Σε−1\mat{G} = \gmat{\Sigma}_{x \mid y} \mat{H}^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1}G=Σx∣y​H⊤Σε−1​, and it lets a transform filter read the same number off its analysis ensemble. dfs_from_gain(gain, obs_matrix) computes the first form. It lies in [0,Dy][0, D_y][0,Dy​], near 0 when the prior dominates and near DyD_yDy​ when the observations do. With an ensemble, the rank of Σ^x\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_xΣ^x​ caps it at min⁡(Dy,NE−1)\min(D_y, N_\mathcal{E} - 1)min(Dy​,NE​−1).

dfs_from_ensemble computes something different, despite its name. With σi,t∣t−12\sigma_{i, t \mid t-1}^2σi,t∣t−12​ the forecast variance of component iii, it returns

∑i=1Dx[X~t∣t⊤X~t∣t−1]ii(NE−1) σi,t∣t−12,\sum_{i = 1}^{D_x} \frac{[\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t}^\top \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t-1}]_{ii}}{(N_\mathcal{E} - 1) \, \sigma_{i, t \mid t-1}^2},i=1∑Dx​​(NE​−1)σi,t∣t−12​[X~t∣t⊤​X~t∣t−1​]ii​​,
(13.15)

the share of the forecast anomalies that survives in the analysis, summed over the state. It is DxD_xDx​ when the observations do nothing, and it falls as they gain influence, which is the opposite direction to (13.14). For a scalar under the ETKF, the transform is 1−g\sqrt{1 - g}1−g​ with gain ggg, so a component contributes 1−g\sqrt{1 - g}1−g​ here and ggg in the DFS. Read it as a measure of retained spread, not as the DFS.

Weight degeneracy¶

Importance-weighted ensembles have two degeneracy monitors Liu & Chen, 1998. For normalised weights wew_ewe​, with ∑ewe=1\sum_e w_e = 1∑e​we​=1,

Neff=1∑ewe2,H[w]=−∑ewelog⁡we.N_\text{eff} = \frac{1}{\sum_e w_e^2}, \qquad \mathbb{H}[\vect{w}] = -\sum_e w_e \log w_e.Neff​=∑e​we2​1​,H[w]=−e∑​we​logwe​.
(13.16)

These are effective_ensemble_size and weight_entropy. Equal weights give Neff=NEN_\text{eff} = N_\mathcal{E}Neff​=NE​ and H=log⁡NE\mathbb{H} = \log N_\mathcal{E}H=logNE​, and one dominant member gives 1 and 0. Since both are Rényi entropies of different orders, Neff≤exp⁡H[w]≤NEN_\text{eff} \le \exp \mathbb{H}[\vect{w}] \le N_\mathcal{E}Neff​≤expH[w]≤NE​.

Neither function normalises its input, and filterax has no particle filter of its own. The mean weights wˉ\bar{\vect{w}}wˉ of chapter 6 are transform coefficients that can be negative, so they are not importance weights either.

It prints:

The last row is the trap, since unnormalised weights give an impossible NeffN_\text{eff}Neff​ below 1, and an entropy that looks like total degeneracy.

Implementation in filterax¶

The first two rows live at the top level of filterax, and the others in filterax.utils. Every utils function takes pre-computed arrays, so none of them runs an analysis.

filters.*.analysis returns log_likelihood on its result, and the Layer 2 assimilate stacks those as log_likelihoods, along with forecast_history and analysis_history. So the departures for the Desroziers functions come straight from those histories, as the next section does. analysis_history holds the ensemble after inflation. That leaves the mean and hence the departures unchanged, and it does change dfs_from_ensemble and any spread read from it.

Algorithm: a health check for a run¶

Program 13.9 runs the checks above together on the Lorenz-96 twin of chapter 6: 20 members without inflation, 40 members without inflation, and 20 members with RTPS. Each row of the table below is the second half of the run.

The first two lines print 1e-14 and 4e-14: the scan reproduces assimilate on the first five windows, both its analysis and its log-likelihood. The rest of the block prints:

Almost every row separates the failed run from the two healthy ones, and three of them need no truth: χ2/Dy\chi^2 / D_yχ2/Dy​, the log-likelihood and the Desroziers estimate. The spread alone does not: at 0.26 it looks fine, and only its ratio to the error or to the innovations reveals the failure. The healthy runs also differ. Forty members without inflation are underdispersive at SSR=0.81\mathrm{SSR} = 0.81SSR=0.81, while RTPS brings 20 members to 1.03 and a much flatter rank histogram. The DFS and dfs_from_ensemble hardly notice the failure, because they describe the update and not its correctness.

Numerics¶

The diagnostics are simple arithmetic with few numerical traps, and the likelihood is where the care goes. Program 13.10 measures three cases in float32. With Σε\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilonΣε​ small against Σ^h\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_hΣ^h​, the Woodbury route loses accuracy, and so the QR route is the one the filters use. The block also checks a likelihood gradient, and the floors that keep ratios finite.

The errors in the float32 log-likelihood, against the float64 reference, print as:

σ2\sigma^2σ2Woodbury routeQR route
16.0e-071.3e-07
10-42.2e-041.2e-07
10-69.8e-033.2e-07

The QR route holds its accuracy across six decades, and that is why the filters report it. The next line prints -1.152792 -1.152792, so the gradient of the likelihood in σ2\sigma^2σ2 matches a central difference. A collapsed component reads as zero in ensemble_spread, printed as [1.414 0. ]. But jnp.std has an infinite slope there, so the gradient of rms_spread holds NaN, printed as True, and a spread-based training loss needs a floor. The floors inside the diagnostics keep the ratios finite. When the mean equals the truth, spread_skill_ratio divides by 10-30 and prints 1e+30, which is a large number and not a meaningful one.

When it breaks¶

The common ways to misread these numbers:

  • One window is not enough: χ2/Dy\chi^2 / D_yχ2/Dy​ has a null standard deviation of 2/Dy\sqrt{2 / D_y}2/Dy​​, so use a running mean.

  • The target is not exactly 1: χ2/Dy\chi^2 / D_yχ2/Dy​, the SSR and the CRPS all have finite-ensemble corrections, measured above.

  • rank_histogram_chi2 assumes independent counts, so on a real run compare it between configurations, as in Program 13.9.

  • Ranking the truth against an observation without noise in the members produces a false U shape, as Program 13.4 measures.

  • The Desroziers functions are not centred, so remove the mean of each departure first if bias is possible, as Program 13.6 shows.

  • desroziers_R_estimate obeys (13.13) on a misspecified run, so one pass only moves towards the true noise.

  • effective_ensemble_size returns a wrong number for unnormalised weights, with no warning, as Program 13.8 prints.

  • dfs_from_ensemble runs the other way from the DFS, as Program 13.7 measures, and it also sees any inflation in analysis_history.

When each one is the right answer¶

Use rms_spread and chi2_normalized in every run, since they need no truth and they catch divergence early. Use log_likelihood or result.log_likelihood to compare configurations on the same observations, and as a training loss. Use rmse_vs_truth, spread_skill_ratio, rank_histogram and crps_ensemble_batch in a twin experiment, where you can verify against the truth. Use the Desroziers functions on an operational record, to check the observation-error covariance you assumed. Use dfs_from_gain to ask how much an observing system contributes, and the form in (13.14) when the filter never forms a gain. Use effective_ensemble_size and weight_entropy only with real importance weights.
